title: Xをしたい vs Xがしたい
summary: Both are fine: が says that X is making you want it; を says that you want to do the action.

blocks.text: The adjective of desire たい points at something. In **パンが食べたい**, it points at the bread: "the bread is want-inducing (to me)". But you also hear **パンを食べたい**. Are the particles changing their meaning? No. They always mean the same thing; only the point of view changes.

rows: the bread is tempting me, right now
I want to do the action "eat bread"

blocks.text: パンが食べたい。 The bread makes me want to eat it.
(私が)パンを食べたい。 I want to eat bread.
How can an adjective have an object? Because たい is attached to the whole unit パンを食べ, not to the verb 食べ alone. We can glue verbs and objects into one block and add たい to it.
When を is the natural choice

With abstract things or people, we do not feel the thing is "pulling" us. It is our own decision: 国を守りたい, 友達を助けたい, 平和を守りたい. It is also more respectful for people: 友達を助けたい, not 友達が助けたい, because the friend is not a tempting object.

blocks.en: I want to help my friend.
I feel like having cold water. (the water tempts me)

blocks.jp: お腹がすいたから、早く食べたい。
blocks.en: I'm hungry, so I want to eat soon. (the adjective points back at me)

items: が + たい: the thing is the cause of the wish.
を + たい: I want to do that action; common with people and abstract things.
The particles never change meaning; the point of view does.
